lede: About twenty-eight days, two hormones and one lining that is built, kept and then lost. Day 1 is the first day of bleeding and day 14 is when an ovum is released; almost everything else in this topic hangs off those two numbers.

Say what oestrogen does and what progesterone does, without swapping them.
Name the two sex hormones, where each is made, and the changes each one causes.

text: Sex hormones and the menstrual cycle

md: Every month the uterus builds a thick lining, keeps it for about a fortnight, and then either uses it or loses it. Two hormones run that cycle: one builds, the other keeps. Learn the calendar first and the chemistry hangs off it.

md:
**Day 1** is the **first day of bleeding** — not the day it stops.

**Days 1 to 5: menstruation.** The lining breaks down and is lost.
**Days 5 to 14: the lining is rebuilt**, thicker each day.
**Day 14: ovulation.** An ovary releases one ovum.
**Days 14 to 28: the lining is kept ready** — progesterone holds it there while it finishes thickening.

prompt: On about which day of a 28-day menstrual cycle does ovulation happen?
explain: Day 14, halfway through a 28-day cycle and a fortnight before the next period would start.

text: 2. Two hormones, and the jobs they never swap

alt: Two rows: the testes make testosterone, which causes a deeper voice, facial and body hair and wider shoulders; the ovaries make oestrogen, which causes the breasts to develop, the hips to widen and the menstrual cycle to begin.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 920 420" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="mc-hormones"><title id="mc-hormones">Two rows: the testes make testosterone, which causes a deeper voice, facial and body hair and wider shoulders; the ovaries make oestrogen, which causes the breasts to develop, the hips to widen and the menstrual cycle to begin</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><ellipse cx="180" cy="150" rx="52" ry="36"/><ellipse cx="180" cy="320" rx="52" ry="34"/><path d="M236 150 H330"/><path d="M330 150 l-9 -4 v8 z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M236 320 H330"/><path d="M330 320 l-9 -4 v8 z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M338 116 H880 V184 H338 z"/><path d="M338 286 H880 V354 H338 z"/></g><g fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.14" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2"><ellipse cx="180" cy="150" rx="52" ry="36"/><ellipse cx="180" cy="320" rx="52" ry="34"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="40" y="34" font-size="13.5" font-weight="600">Two sex hormones, two places they are made</text><text x="40" y="54" font-size="11.5">Name the gland and you have named the hormone.</text><text x="180" y="154" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12">testes</text><text x="180" y="324" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12">ovaries</text><text x="352" y="144" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">testosterone</text><text x="352" y="166" font-size="11.5">deeper voice, facial and body hair, wider shoulders, sperm production begins</text><text x="352" y="314" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">oestrogen</text><text x="352" y="336" font-size="11.5">breasts develop, hips widen, body hair grows, the menstrual cycle begins</text><text x="40" y="400" font-size="11.5">Both are called secondary sexual characteristics: the changes that appear at puberty.</text></g></svg>
caption: Name the gland and you have named the hormone.

md:
**Oestrogen**, from the **ovaries**, **repairs and thickens** the lining after menstruation.
**Progesterone** **maintains** that lining through the second half of the cycle.

Three words hold the whole cycle: **build, maintain, shed**. Oestrogen builds. Progesterone maintains. When progesterone falls, the lining sheds.

**Testosterone**, from the **testes**, and oestrogen also cause the **secondary sexual characteristics** at puberty.

title: GCSE Biology - The Menstrual Cycle & Puberty (2027/28 exams)
why: Watch it for the puberty and secondary-characteristics half, which is exactly this section. It is made for another board, so it spends a long time on two hormones called FSH and LH that CCEA does not examine — you can let those pass.

prompt: Oestrogen repairs and thickens the lining of the uterus. Which hormone maintains it afterwards?
explain: Progesterone. Examiners report that its spelling is very varied, so type it once more now while it costs nothing.

title: Read the timing, not the height
md:
Oestrogen peaks at about day 13, just **before** ovulation; progesterone peaks about a week **after** it, at day 21. Follow the day-14 line down and you can see the lining is already thick by then.

The hormone axis has **no numbers**, and it is not meant to. You can say when each curve rises, peaks and falls. You cannot say one hormone is "higher" than the other, because nothing on that axis compares them.

prompt: On the lower graph of the 28-day cycle, the lining is read in millimetres. What is its thickness on day 20?
explain: 10.0 mm. Go up from day 20 to the curve, then straight across to the millimetre scale.

text: 4. A worked reading, mark by mark

alt: An ultrasound scan of an ovary showing one large dark circular follicle close to the surface, measured across by two pairs of callipers.
credit: Luis F. Goncalves, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
caption: A real ovary scanned a day or two before ovulation. The dark circle is the fluid-filled space holding the ovum.
prompt: Roughly which day of the cycle would this scan have been taken, and what happens to this structure within about two days?

title: Worked example: 'Calculate the increase in the thickness of the lining between day 5 and day 24. [2]'
md:
**Step 1 — read day 5.** Up to the curve, across to the scale: **1.0 mm**. Write it down before you look for the second one. **[1]**
**Step 2 — read day 24.** Same method: **12.0 mm**.
**Step 3 — subtract, later minus earlier.** 12.0 − 1.0 = **11.0 mm**. **[1]**

The other way round gives a negative number for something that grew, and that is the commonest slip on this part.

prompt: Using the same graph of the 28-day cycle: the lining is 1.0 mm on day 5 and 10.0 mm on day 20. By how many millimetres has it grown?
explain: 10.0 − 1.0 = 9.0 mm. Later value minus earlier value, so a growth comes out positive.

caption: The same four stages, but ovulation has slid to day 17.

md:
Cycles vary. What stays almost fixed is the gap **after** ovulation: about **14 days** from ovulation to the next period.

So count **back** from the end, never forward from day 1. For a cycle of 31 days: 31 − 14 = **day 17**.

A longer cycle ovulates later; a shorter one ovulates earlier. Day 14 is only the answer for a 28-day cycle.

prompt: A woman's cycle lasts 30 days. Ovulation happens about 14 days before the end of a cycle. On about which day does she ovulate?
explain: 30 − 14 = day 16. Count back from the end of the cycle.

md:
Fertilisation is most likely **around ovulation**, because that is the only time an ovum is in the oviduct waiting.

On **day 3** almost nothing is possible: no ovum has been released, and the lining is breaking down, so nothing could implant even if it were.

Those 5 days are about 16% of a 31-day cycle — a small window, and the whole basis of the next topic.

prompt: Why is fertilisation very unlikely on day 3 of a 28-day cycle?
options: no ovum has been released yet
answer: no ovum has been released yet
explain: Ovulation is still eleven days away on day 3, and menstruation is breaking the lining down at the same time.

md:
Give the day numbers: menstruation **days 1 to 5**, ovulation **about day 14**, with day 1 the first day of bleeding.
Say that **oestrogen repairs and thickens** the lining and **progesterone maintains** it — build, maintain, shed.
Name **testosterone** and **oestrogen**, where each is made, and the **secondary sexual characteristics** each causes.
Read a thickness or a day off the cycle graph, and say why the hormone heights cannot be compared.
Work out the day of ovulation in a cycle that is **not** 28 days long.

This is an early question worth about **five to seven marks**, usually opened by a graph of the uterus lining. The first mark is a day number read off it; the last is normally a hormone named or a role given. Stuck? Write the verb: oestrogen **thickens**, progesterone **maintains**. Spell progesterone slowly — it is a key word, so it has to be readable.
